Arrays & hashing.summary: Trade memory for time: remember what you have seen in a hash map or set.
signals: "Find a pair / duplicate / complement" in an unsorted array
Group items that share a key (anagrams, same digits)
"Have I seen this before?" in one pass
O(n) is expected and sorting is not allowed or too slow
Arrays & hashing.idea: Walk the array once and keep a hash map from a key (the value, its complement, a sorted signature) to what you need later: an index, a count, or a list. Each lookup is O(1) on average, so a nested O(n²) search becomes one pass.
Arrays & hashing.example: Two sum: return the indexes of two values that add up to target.
bugs: Storing the value before checking it, so an item pairs with itself.
Using a list instead of a set or map for lookups (O(n) each).
Using mutable keys (a list) instead of a tuple or string.
Forgetting that several items can share a key: keep a list or a count.

Two pointers.summary: Two indexes move toward each other (or in the same direction), each step ruling something out.
signals: The array is sorted (or you may sort it)
Find a pair or triple with a target sum, or the best pair (most water)
Reverse, compare from both ends, or check a palindrome
Remove or compact items in place with O(1) extra space
Two pointers.idea: Put one pointer at each end. Look at the pair: if the sum is too small, only moving the left pointer right can help; if too big, move the right pointer left. Each step throws one value away for good, so the scan is O(n). The same-direction form uses a slow write index and a fast read index to compact an array in place.
Two pointers.example: Pair with a target sum in a sorted array (return the two indexes).

code.python:
def pair_with_sum(a, target):          # a is sorted
    i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
    while i < j:                       # i < j: never pair an item with itself
        s = a[i] + a[j]
        if s == target:                # CHANGE: what counts as an answer
            return [i, j]
        if s < target:
            i += 1                     # need a bigger sum
        else:
            j -= 1                     # need a smaller sum
    return [-1, -1]

Two pointers.complexity: O(n) time after sorting (O(n log n) if you must sort), O(1) extra space.
bugs: Using i <= j so an item pairs with itself.
Forgetting to sort first, or losing the original indexes when you sort.
For 3Sum: not skipping equal neighbours, so the same triple appears twice.
Moving both pointers when only one side is ruled out.

Sliding window.summary: Grow a window on the right, shrink it on the left while it is invalid, and record the best valid window.
signals: "Longest / shortest substring or subarray such that ..."
The condition is about what is inside a contiguous range (distinct letters, sum, counts)
Adding an item can only make the window "more invalid" (monotone condition)
All values positive (for sums), so shrinking always lowers the sum
Sliding window.idea: Move right one step at a time and add that item to a count map. While the window breaks the rule, remove the item at left and move left forward. After the loop the window is valid, so record it. Both pointers only move forward, so it is O(n). For the shortest valid window, record inside the shrink loop instead.
Sliding window.example: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters.

code.python:
def longest_at_most_k(s, k):
    count, left, best = {}, 0, 0
    for right, c in enumerate(s):
        count[c] = count.get(c, 0) + 1         # grow: add s[right]
        while len(count) > k:                  # CHANGE: while the window is invalid
            d = s[left]
            count[d] -= 1
            if count[d] == 0:
                del count[d]
            left += 1                          # shrink
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)     # valid again: record
    return best

bugs: Recording before the window is valid again (record after the while loop).
Not deleting a key whose count drops to 0, so len(count) is wrong.
Using a sliding window when values can be negative: use prefix sums instead.
For the shortest window: recording after the loop instead of inside it.

Stack.summary: Push what is still open; pop when its partner arrives.
signals: Matching pairs: brackets, tags, open and close
Evaluate an expression or decode nested text ("3[a2[c]]")
Undo the most recent thing first (backspace, asteroid collisions)
Keep a running minimum next to each pushed value (min stack)
Stack.idea: A stack remembers unfinished work in the order it must be finished: the most recent open item is closed first. Push each opening item; when a closing item comes, the top of the stack must be its partner, so pop and check. At the end the stack must be empty.
Stack.example: Valid parentheses: every bracket is closed by the same kind, in the right order.
bugs: Popping from an empty stack when a closer arrives first.
Forgetting to check that the stack is empty at the end.
For nested decoding: not saving the outer state (count and partial string) on the stack.
Using a queue (first in, first out) by mistake.

Monotonic stack.summary: Keep a stack whose values only go down (or up); each new item pops everything it beats.
signals: "Next greater / smaller element" for every position
How far can each item reach left or right before something blocks it (spans, histogram)
Remove digits or letters to make the smallest result
Sum over all subarrays of their minimum or maximum
Monotonic stack.idea: Scan once and keep indexes on a stack whose values are decreasing. When a new value is bigger than the top, the top has found its next greater element: pop it and record the answer. Keep popping while that holds, then push the new index. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total work is O(n).
Monotonic stack.example: Next greater element to the right of each value (-1 if none).

code.python:
def next_greater(a):
    ans = [-1] * len(a)
    stack = []                           # indexes; their values go down
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:    # CHANGE: < for greater, > for smaller
            ans[stack.pop()] = x             # x answers the popped index
        stack.append(i)
    return ans                           # indexes left on the stack keep -1

bugs: Pushing values instead of indexes, so you cannot compute distances.
Using < instead of <= (or the other way) and mishandling equal values.
Forgetting the items left on the stack at the end (their answer is the default).
For circular arrays: loop twice over the indexes (i % n).

Binary search.summary: Halve a sorted range each step by asking a yes/no question about the middle.
signals: The input is sorted, or rotated sorted, or "increases then decreases"
"First / last position", "insert position", lower bound
O(log n) is required
A yes/no test that is false and then true along the index (monotone)
Binary search.idea: Think of a test ok(i) that is false for small i and true from some point on. Keep lo..hi so the first true index is always inside; look at the middle and drop the half that cannot contain it. Writing every search as "find the first true" avoids most off-by-one errors.
Binary search.example: Lower bound: the first index whose value is >= target (len(a) if none).
Binary search.complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) extra space.
bugs: Infinite loop: with lo < hi and hi = mid, use mid = (lo + hi) // 2 (rounded down).
Overflow of lo + hi in fixed-width languages: use lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
Wrong initial hi: it must be able to hold "not found" (len(a)).
A test that is not monotone, so the search has no meaning.

Linked lists.summary: Rewire next pointers one node at a time, keeping a pointer to what you would otherwise lose.
signals: Reverse a list or part of it, or reorder nodes
Merge sorted lists, or split one list in two
Remove the n-th node from the end (two pointers n apart)
O(1) extra space: you must change links, not copy values
Linked lists.idea: Walk the list with prev and cur. Before you change cur.next, save the next node, because changing the link loses it. A dummy node in front of the head removes the special case for the first node when you insert or delete.
bugs: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting cur.next before saving it.
Returning the old head instead of prev.
Special-casing the head instead of using a dummy node.
Creating a cycle by forgetting to cut the old link.

Trees & BST.summary: Breadth-first by levels with a queue, or depth-first with recursion; in a BST, inorder is sorted.
signals: "Level by level", "right side view", "zigzag", "minimum depth"
Depth, balance, same tree, lowest common ancestor
Validate a BST (each node within a min/max range from its ancestors)
Anything "per level" needs BFS; anything "per subtree" needs DFS
Trees & BST.idea: For levels: put the root in a queue; at each round, read how many nodes the queue holds now (that is one level), pop exactly that many and push their children. For subtree questions use DFS (see Tree DFS with return values). For a BST, pass down the allowed (low, high) range or use the fact that inorder visits values in sorted order.
Trees & BST.example: Level order traversal: the values of each level, top to bottom.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):                 # node: .val, .left, .right
    if not root:
        return []
    out, q = [], deque([root])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):        # exactly the nodes of this level
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)     # CHANGE: what to do with each node
            if node.left:
                q.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                q.append(node.right)
        out.append(level)
    return out

Trees & BST.complexity: O(n) time, O(width) queue space for BFS; O(height) stack space for DFS.
bugs: Not snapshotting the level size, so levels mix.
Checking only parent vs child when validating a BST (the whole range matters).
Pushing null children into the queue.
Recursion depth on a very deep tree in Python: use an explicit stack.

Heaps & top-K.summary: A heap gives the smallest (or largest) item in O(log n); keep only k items in it.
signals: "k largest / smallest / most frequent / closest"
Merge k sorted lists or streams
A running median, or repeatedly take the best remaining item
Scheduling: always pick the job with the earliest end or highest priority
Heaps & top-K.idea: For the k largest, keep a min-heap of size k: push each item and pop when the heap grows past k. The heap then holds the k largest, and its top is the k-th largest. That is O(n log k) time and O(k) space, better than sorting when k is small. Flip the order (or negate values) for the k smallest.
Heaps & top-K.example: The k-th largest value in an array.
Heaps & top-K.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) extra space.
bugs: Using a max-heap of all n items (O(n log n)) when a size-k min-heap is enough.
Python's heapq is a min-heap: negate values for a max-heap.
Comparing tuples whose second field is not comparable: add a counter as a tie-breaker.
Popping before pushing and losing a candidate.

Intervals.summary: Sort by start, then sweep once, merging or comparing each interval with the last kept one.
signals: A list of [start, end] ranges: meetings, bookings, segments
Merge overlapping ranges, insert a range, find free time
Do any two overlap? Intersections of two lists
Remove the fewest intervals to make the rest non-overlapping (sort by end)
Intervals.idea: Sort the intervals by start. Then each new interval either overlaps the last merged one (its start is not after that end), so extend the end with max, or it starts a new group. One pass after the sort. For "keep the most non-overlapping" problems sort by end instead and greedily keep each interval that starts after the last kept end.
Intervals.complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) for the output.
bugs: Setting the merged end to the new end instead of max(old end, new end).
Touching intervals ([1,2] and [2,3]): decide whether they count as overlapping.
Sorting by end when the problem needs start (or the other way).
Modifying the input list while iterating over it.

Greedy.summary: Sort by the right key, then take each item if it still fits; prove that the local choice is never worse.
signals: "Maximum number of non-overlapping ...", "minimum arrows / platforms"
"Can you reach the end?" with jump lengths (track the farthest reach)
One pass with a running best (buy low, sell high)
An exchange argument works: swapping in the greedy choice never hurts
Greedy.idea: Find the order in which an early choice can never block a better solution, often by earliest end time, and take items in that order whenever they fit. Check it with an exchange argument: in any optimal answer you can swap the first choice for the greedy one without making it worse. If you cannot argue that, the problem probably needs DP.
Greedy.example: Activity selection: the most intervals that do not overlap (sort by end).

code.python:
def max_non_overlapping(intervals):
    count, end = 0, float("-inf")
    for s, e in sorted(intervals, key=lambda iv: iv[1]):   # CHANGE: the greedy order
        if s >= end:                       # CHANGE: does it still fit?
            count += 1
            end = e                        # take it
    return count

Greedy.complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(1) extra space.
bugs: Sorting by start (or length) when the proof needs the end.
Using greedy where it fails (0/1 knapsack, coin systems like {1, 3, 4}): test small cases.
Strict vs non-strict comparison for touching intervals.
Not handling an empty input.

Backtracking.summary: Choose, explore, un-choose: walk the tree of partial answers and prune branches that cannot work.
signals: "All" subsets, permutations, combinations, partitions, boards
Small n (up to about 15 to 20) and exponential output
Place items under constraints (N-Queens, Sudoku, word search)
"Without duplicates" in the output: sort and skip equal siblings
Backtracking.idea: Keep one path (the partial answer). At each level loop over the choices: add one to the path, recurse, then remove it so the next choice starts clean. Record a copy of the path when it is complete. Prune as early as possible: skip a choice equal to the previous sibling (after sorting), or stop when the partial sum is already too big.
Backtracking.example: Subsets II: all subsets of a list that may contain duplicates, each subset once.
Backtracking.complexity: O(2^n · n) time in the worst case (the number of answers times the copy), O(n) recursion depth.
bugs: Appending the path itself instead of a copy, so every answer ends up the same.
Forgetting to un-choose (pop) after the recursive call.
Skipping duplicates with i > 0 instead of i > start (that skips valid answers).
Not sorting before the duplicate check.

Graphs.summary: Breadth-first search from a start node: the first time you reach a node is by the fewest edges.
signals: Nodes and edges, possibly hidden (words that differ by one letter, cities, users)
"Fewest steps / moves / transformations" when every step costs the same
Connected or not, how many groups, which nodes can reach which
Build the adjacency list first, then search
Graphs.idea: Build an adjacency list. BFS keeps a queue of nodes in the order they were found; mark a node as seen when you put it in the queue, not when you take it out, so it is queued once. Because the queue holds nodes in order of distance, the first time a node is seen its distance is the shortest number of edges. O(V + E).
Graphs.example: Shortest number of edges from start to every node in an unweighted graph (-1 if unreachable).

code.python:
from collections import deque

def bfs_dist(n, edges, start):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v in edges:                     # CHANGE: how neighbours are found
        adj[u].append(v)
        adj[v].append(u)                   # undirected: both ways
    dist = [-1] * n
    dist[start] = 0
    q = deque([start])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        for v in adj[u]:
            if dist[v] == -1:              # not seen yet
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1      # mark when queued
                q.append(v)
    return dist

bugs: Marking nodes as seen when popping, so the same node is queued many times.
Using DFS for shortest paths (DFS does not give the fewest edges).
Forgetting nodes that have no edges when you build the adjacency list.
For undirected graphs, adding the edge only one way.

Topological sort.summary: Repeatedly take a node with no remaining prerequisites (Kahn's algorithm).
signals: Tasks with prerequisites, build order, course schedule
"Is there a cycle in this directed graph?"
An order consistent with pairwise rules (alien dictionary)
Shortest number of rounds / semesters (BFS by levels of in-degree 0)
Topological sort.idea: Count incoming edges (in-degree) for each node. Put every node with in-degree 0 in a queue. Pop one, add it to the order, and remove its outgoing edges by lowering its neighbours' in-degrees; a neighbour that reaches 0 joins the queue. If the order ends shorter than the number of nodes, the rest sit on a cycle.
Topological sort.example: An order of n courses given prerequisite pairs (a, b) meaning a before b; [] if impossible.

code.python:
from collections import deque

def topo_order(n, edges):                  # edge (a, b): a must come before b
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:
        adj[a].append(b)
        indeg[b] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    order = []
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        order.append(u)                    # CHANGE: what to do when u is ready
        for v in adj[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return order if len(order) == n else []   # shorter: there is a cycle

bugs: Getting the edge direction backwards (prerequisite -> course).
Forgetting the cycle check (order shorter than n).
Leaving out nodes with no edges at all.
Counting a duplicate edge twice in in-degree but adding it once to the list (or the reverse).

Union-find.summary: Each group is a tree; find walks to the root, union links two roots.
signals: Merge items into groups as you read pairs (accounts, friends, equal variables)
"Number of connected components" with edges arriving over time
Does this new edge close a cycle? (redundant connection, Kruskal)
Grouping by a shared key (same email, same row or column)
Union-find.idea: Keep parent[x] for each item; the root of its tree names the group. find(x) follows parents to the root and, with path compression, points every visited node straight at it. union(a, b) links the smaller tree's root under the larger one's. Together these make each operation almost O(1).
Union-find.example: Count connected components while adding edges; report edges that close a cycle.
Union-find.complexity: Almost O(1) per operation (inverse Ackermann), O(n) space.
bugs: Linking a and b instead of their roots.
Forgetting path compression or union by size, making long chains (O(n) finds).
Recursive find hitting the recursion limit: write it iteratively.
Not decreasing the component count only when the roots differ.

Shortest paths.summary: Dijkstra: always settle the closest unsettled node, using a min-heap of (distance, node).
signals: Weighted edges, all weights >= 0: cheapest / fastest / most reliable path
"Minimum effort / cost" where a path's cost combines its edges (sum, max)
At most k stops: Bellman-Ford rounds or BFS on (node, stops)
Edge weights 0 or 1 only: a deque (0-1 BFS) is enough
Shortest paths.idea: Keep a min-heap of (best known distance, node). Pop the smallest; if it is stale (larger than the distance already stored), skip it. Otherwise it is final: relax each edge, and push a neighbour whenever its distance improves. With a binary heap this is O((V + E) log V). It breaks with negative weights.
Shortest paths.example: Cheapest distance from a source to every node in a directed graph with non-negative weights.

code.python:
import heapq

def dijkstra(n, edges, src):               # edges: (u, v, w), directed, w >= 0
    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        adj[u].append((v, w))
    dist = [float("inf")] * n
    dist[src] = 0
    heap = [(0, src)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                       # stale entry
        for v, w in adj[u]:
            nd = d + w                     # CHANGE: how a path's cost grows
            if nd < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = nd
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nd, v))
    return dist

Shortest paths.complexity: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space.
bugs: Not skipping stale heap entries, which repeats work (still correct, but slow).
Using Dijkstra with negative edges.
Marking a node done when pushing instead of when popping.
Overflow when adding to an "infinite" distance: check for infinity first.

1-D DP.summary: dp[i] is the answer for the first i items (or amount i), built from a few smaller answers.
signals: "Number of ways", "minimum cost", "maximum value" along a line of choices
Each step depends on the last one or two steps (stairs, robber, decode ways)
Plain recursion would solve the same sub-problem many times
Coin change, word break, longest increasing subsequence
1-D DP.idea: Define dp[i] in words first ("the most money from the first i houses"). Write the recurrence from the last choice (rob house i or not), set the base cases, and fill i from small to large so every value you need is ready. When dp[i] only uses dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], keep two variables instead of the array.
1-D DP.example: House robber: the most money from houses in a row, never robbing two neighbours.
1-D DP.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space with rolling variables.
bugs: Not writing down what dp[i] means, then mixing up "first i" and "ending at i".
Wrong base cases (dp[0] for zero items).
Updating the rolling variables in the wrong order.
Recursing without a memo (exponential time).

2-D DP.summary: dp[i][j] combines two indexes (two prefixes, a position and a budget); fill row by row.
signals: Two strings or two sequences compared position by position
A grid or a (item, capacity) pair as the state
"Longest common ...", "number of paths", "largest square"
The state needs two numbers to be described
2-D DP.idea: Choose what dp[i][j] means, usually about the first i items of one input and the first j of the other. Each cell looks at a few neighbours (up, left, diagonal), so fill the table in an order where those are already done, normally row by row. Size the table (n+1) × (m+1) so row 0 and column 0 are the empty cases.
2-D DP.example: Longest common subsequence of two strings.
2-D DP.complexity: O(n · m) time, O(n · m) space (O(m) with two rolling rows).
bugs: Off by one between dp indexes and string indexes (dp[i] uses s[i-1]).
Filling in an order where a needed neighbour is still empty.
Allocating rows that share the same list ([[0]*m]*n in Python).
Not initialising row 0 and column 0.

Tries & strings.summary: A tree of characters: words with a common prefix share a path, so prefix questions cost O(word length).
signals: "Starts with", autocomplete, search suggestions
Many words searched in a grid or a text at once (word search II)
Replace words by their shortest root, count words with a prefix
Wildcard search ('.' matches any letter): DFS over the trie
Tries & strings.idea: Each node has up to one child per letter and an end flag. insert walks the word, creating missing children, and marks the last node. search walks the word and needs the end flag; startsWith only needs the path to exist. Store a counter in each node to answer "how many words have this prefix" in O(prefix length).
Tries & strings.example: A trie with insert, search, startsWith and a prefix count.
Tries & strings.complexity: O(L) per operation for a word of length L; O(total letters) space.
bugs: Returning true from search for a word that is only a prefix (check the end flag).
Sharing one children map between nodes by mistake.
Not pruning found words in word search II, so the same word is reported many times.
Using a 26-array for non-lowercase input.

Bit manipulation.summary: Use the bits of an integer directly: XOR cancels pairs, n & (n - 1) drops the lowest set bit.
signals: Every value appears twice except one (XOR everything)
Count set bits, powers of two, single bit flags
Add without + (carry = a & b shifted left)
Enumerate all subsets of a small set with a mask
Bit manipulation.idea: XOR is its own inverse, so x ^ x = 0 and pairs cancel. n & (n - 1) clears the lowest 1 bit, so a loop over it runs once per set bit. (1 << i) builds a mask for bit i; mask & (1 << i) tests it; mask | (1 << i) sets it. For "three times except one", count each bit position mod 3.
Bit manipulation.example: Single number: every value appears twice except one.

code.python:
def single_number(nums):
    x = 0
    for v in nums:
        x ^= v                             # pairs cancel: v ^ v == 0
    return x

def count_bits(n):                         # number of 1 bits (n >= 0)
    c = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1                         # drop the lowest 1 bit
        c += 1
    return c

def all_subsets(items):                    # each mask is one subset
    n = len(items)
    return [[items[i] for i in range(n) if mask & (1 << i)] for mask in range(1 << n)]

Bit manipulation.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space; bit loops are O(number of bits).
bugs: Operator precedence: in many languages a & b == c means a & (b == c).
Signed right shift on negative numbers (use unsigned / >>> in JavaScript).
JavaScript bit operators work on 32-bit signed integers.
Python integers are unbounded: mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF to imitate 32 bits.

Design.summary: Combine two structures so every operation is O(1) or O(log n): a hash map for lookup plus an ordered structure.
signals: "Design a class with get / put / ... in O(1)" (LRU, LFU, random set)
Evict the least recently or least frequently used item
Rate limiters, hit counters, time-based key-value stores
Each operation must stay fast as the data grows
Design.idea: List the operations and the cost each must have, then pick one structure per need: a hash map to find an item, plus a doubly linked list (order of use), a heap (priority), an array with swap-remove (random pick) or a sorted list per key (timestamps). Keep the two structures in sync in every operation. For LRU, a map from key to list node lets you move a node to the front in O(1).
Design.example: LRU cache with get and put in O(1).
bugs: Updating the map but not the order (or the other way) on get or put.
Evicting before inserting when the key already exists.
Capacity 0 or 1 edge cases.
Using a list scan to find an item (O(n)).

Prefix sums.summary: Store running totals once; any range sum is then one subtraction.
signals: Many range-sum queries on an array that does not change
"Number of subarrays whose sum is k" (negatives allowed)
Equal counts of two kinds (map them to +1 and -1)
Product or sum of everything except index i
Prefix sums.idea: P[k] is the sum of the first k values, so sum(a[l..r]) = P[r+1] - P[l]. To count subarrays with sum k, walk once and keep a hash map from each prefix sum seen so far to how often it appeared; every earlier prefix equal to sum - k starts one such subarray. Start the map with {0: 1} for subarrays that begin at index 0.
Prefix sums.example: Count the subarrays whose sum equals k.
Prefix sums.complexity: O(n) time, O(n) extra space; each range query O(1).
bugs: Forgetting the starting {0: 1}, so subarrays from index 0 are missed.
Off by one: P has n + 1 entries, and the range is P[r+1] - P[l].
Adding the current prefix to the map before the lookup (counts empty subarrays when k = 0).
Integer overflow on long arrays: use 64-bit sums.

Matrices.summary: Index arithmetic on a 2-D grid: layers, transposes and in-place marks.
signals: Rotate an image 90 degrees in place
Spiral order or layer-by-layer walks
Set rows / columns to zero, Game of Life (update in place)
Search a matrix sorted by rows and columns (start at a corner)
Matrices.idea: Many matrix tricks are two simple moves combined. A 90° clockwise rotation is a transpose (swap a[i][j] with a[j][i]) followed by reversing each row. A spiral walks the outer layer with four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and moves them inward. To update in place, store the new state in spare bits or in the first row and column.
Matrices.example: Rotate an n × n matrix 90 degrees clockwise, in place.

code.python:
def rotate(m):                             # n x n, clockwise, in place
    n = len(m)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):          # transpose: j starts after i
            m[i][j], m[j][i] = m[j][i], m[i][j]
    for row in m:
        row.reverse()                      # CHANGE: reverse columns instead for counter-clockwise
code.scala:
def rotate(m: Array[Array[Int]]): Unit = {      // n x n, clockwise, in place
  val n = m.length
  for (i <- 0 until n; j <- i + 1 until n) {     // transpose
    val t = m(i)(j); m(i)(j) = m(j)(i); m(j)(i) = t
  }
  for (i <- 0 until n) m(i) = m(i).reverse       // CHANGE: direction
}

bugs: Transposing the whole matrix (j from 0) and swapping every pair back.
Reversing columns instead of rows (that rotates the other way).
Spiral: not checking top <= bottom and left <= right before the last two sides.
Reading cells that were already overwritten in this step (Game of Life).

BFS on grids & implicit graphs.summary: BFS where the nodes are cells or states, generated on the fly; start from every source at once.
signals: Shortest number of moves on a grid, board or lock (each move costs 1)
Distance from the nearest of many sources (0s, gates, rotten oranges)
The graph is not given: neighbours are "one move away" states
"Minimum time until everything is reached"
BFS on grids & implicit graphs.idea: Each state (a cell, a lock combination, a board) is a node; its neighbours are the states one move away. Put every source in the queue at distance 0 (multi-source BFS), then expand level by level. The first time a state is reached is by the fewest moves. Keep a seen set of states, encoded as tuples or strings.
BFS on grids & implicit graphs.example: Distance from each open cell to the nearest source cell (multi-source BFS).

code.python:
from collections import deque

def dist_to_nearest(grid):                 # grid: 0 = source, 1 = open, 2 = wall
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    dist = [[-1] * C for _ in range(R)]
    q = deque()
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            if grid[r][c] == 0:            # CHANGE: every source starts at distance 0
                dist[r][c] = 0
                q.append((r, c))
    while q:
        r, c = q.popleft()
        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):   # CHANGE: the moves
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and dist[nr][nc] == -1 and grid[nr][nc] != 2:
                dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1
                q.append((nr, nc))
    return dist

BFS on grids & implicit graphs.complexity: O(rows · cols) time and space (O(states · moves) for implicit graphs).
bugs: Starting BFS from each source separately (O(k · n)) instead of all at once.
Marking seen on pop instead of on push.
Forgetting walls or bounds checks.
States that are hard to hash: encode them as tuples or strings.

Binary search on the answer.summary: Binary search over possible answers, testing each guess with a quick simulation.
signals: "Minimum capacity / speed / time such that ..." or "maximize the minimum"
If a value works, every bigger (or smaller) value also works
Checking one candidate is easy (greedy pass), but finding the best directly is hard
The answer range is large (up to 10^9), so trying each value is too slow
Binary search on the answer.idea: Find the smallest value x for which feasible(x) is true. Set lo and hi to the smallest and largest possible answers, then binary search: if feasible(mid), the answer is mid or smaller; otherwise it is above mid. Each test is a greedy simulation, so the cost is O(n · log(range)).
Binary search on the answer.example: Smallest ship capacity that ships all packages, in order, within d days.
Binary search on the answer.complexity: O(n log(sum)) time, O(1) extra space.
bugs: lo too small (below the largest single item), so feasible() can never succeed.
A feasible() that is not monotone in x.
Off by one between "first true" and "last true" when maximizing.
Overflow when hi is a large sum: use 64-bit.

Tree DFS with return values.summary: A recursive helper returns one value to its parent and updates a global best on the way.
signals: Diameter, longest path, maximum path sum (the path may bend at any node)
"For every subtree": height, sum, tilt, balanced?
Root-to-leaf paths with a target sum
The answer at a node depends on the answers of its children
Tree DFS with return values.idea: Write dfs(node) that returns what the parent needs (often a height or the best one-sided path). Inside, call dfs on both children first (post-order), combine their answers to update a global best for the path that bends at this node, then return only one side upward, because a path through the parent cannot use both.
Tree DFS with return values.example: Diameter of a binary tree: the number of edges on the longest path.

code.python:
def diameter(root):                    # node: .val, .left, .right
    best = 0
    def dfs(node):                     # returns the height in nodes
        nonlocal best
        if not node:
            return 0                   # CHANGE: the value for an empty tree
        L, R = dfs(node.left), dfs(node.right)
        best = max(best, L + R)        # CHANGE: the path that bends here
        return 1 + max(L, R)           # CHANGE: one side only, for the parent
    dfs(root)
    return best

bugs: Returning the bent path (left + right) to the parent instead of one side.
Forgetting the global best, so paths that do not pass the root are missed.
Wrong base value for null (0 for heights, -infinity for sums that must contain a node).
For max path sum: not dropping negative branches with max(0, child).

Graph DFS.summary: Go deep from a node, marking what you visit; each fresh start is a new connected group.
signals: Count or label connected regions (islands, provinces, enclosed areas)
Flood fill, or copy / clone a graph
"Can I reach ..." when the path length does not matter
Mark everything connected to the border first (surrounded regions)
Graph DFS.idea: For every cell or node not yet visited, start a DFS that marks everything reachable from it; one start = one region. Mark a cell before you visit its neighbours so nothing is visited twice. Use an explicit stack when the region can be very large, to avoid deep recursion.
Graph DFS.example: Number of islands in a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water).

code.python:
def num_islands(grid):                     # grid: list of lists of "0" / "1"
    R, C = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    seen = [[False] * C for _ in range(R)]
    def dfs(r, c):                         # explicit stack: no deep recursion
        stack = [(r, c)]
        seen[r][c] = True
        while stack:
            r, c = stack.pop()
            for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= nr < R and 0 <= nc < C and not seen[nr][nc] and grid[nr][nc] == "1":   # CHANGE
                    seen[nr][nc] = True    # mark before visiting
                    stack.append((nr, nc))
    count = 0
    for r in range(R):
        for c in range(C):
            if grid[r][c] == "1" and not seen[r][c]:
                count += 1                 # a new region
                dfs(r, c)
    return count

Graph DFS.complexity: O(rows · cols) time, O(rows · cols) worst-case stack.
bugs: Marking after the recursive calls, so cells are visited again and again (or forever).
Not checking bounds before reading grid[r][c].
Recursion depth limits on big grids (Python): use a stack.
Changing the input grid when the caller still needs it: copy it or use a seen set.

Fixed-length sliding window.summary: A window of exactly k items: add the one entering, drop the one leaving, record.
signals: "Every subarray / substring of length k"
Maximum or average of k consecutive items
Anagram or permutation of a pattern inside a string (window = pattern length)
Take k items from the two ends (= drop a middle window of n - k)
Fixed-length sliding window.idea: Keep a running summary (sum, counts) of the last k items. Each step adds the item entering on the right and removes the item that leaves on the left (index right - k), so each window costs O(1) to update instead of O(k) to rebuild.
Fixed-length sliding window.example: Largest sum of any k consecutive values.
Fixed-length sliding window.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (O(alphabet) for counts).
bugs: Removing the leaving item at the wrong index (it is right - k).
Recording before the first full window (right < k - 1).
k larger than the array: decide what to return.
Rebuilding the window from scratch each step (O(n·k)).

All-pairs shortest paths.summary: Floyd–Warshall: allow one more middle node at a time and improve every pair through it.
signals: Distances between every pair of nodes, n up to a few hundred
"Within distance d of how many cities"
Answering many queries on the same small graph
Ratios or reachability between all pairs (evaluate division, transitive closure)
All-pairs shortest paths.idea: dist[i][j] starts as the direct edge weight (0 on the diagonal, infinity when there is no edge). For each node k in turn, let every path also pass through k: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). After all k, every pair has its shortest distance. The k loop must be the outermost one.
All-pairs shortest paths.example: Shortest distances between all pairs in a weighted graph with n nodes.

code.python:
def floyd_warshall(n, edges):              # edges: (u, v, w), directed
    INF = float("inf")
    dist = [[0 if i == j else INF for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
    for u, v, w in edges:
        dist[u][v] = min(dist[u][v], w)    # undirected: set dist[v][u] too
    for k in range(n):                     # k outermost
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                if dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]:   # CHANGE: how paths combine
                    dist[i][j] = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]
    return dist

bugs: Putting the k loop inside instead of outside.
Adding to infinity and overflowing: check before adding.
Forgetting dist[i][i] = 0.
Using it on large sparse graphs where n Dijkstras would be faster.

Fast and slow pointers.summary: One pointer moves one step, the other two: they meet in a cycle, or the slow one stops at the middle.
signals: A linked list or a "next" function may loop (cycle, happy number)
Find the middle of a list in one pass
Find a duplicate in an array of 1..n without extra memory
O(1) extra space is required
Fast and slow pointers.idea: Move slow by one and fast by two. If there is a cycle, fast gains one step per move inside it and must land on slow. Then restart one pointer from the start and move both by one: they meet at the cycle's entrance, because the tail length equals the distance from the meeting point to the entrance (plus whole laps).
Fast and slow pointers.example: Find where a cycle starts when node i points to nxt[i] (-1 = end of list).

code.python:
def cycle_start(nxt, head):
    step = lambda i: nxt[i] if i != -1 else -1     # CHANGE: how to go to the next node
    slow = fast = head
    while fast != -1 and step(fast) != -1:
        slow, fast = step(slow), step(step(fast))
        if slow == fast:                           # met inside the cycle
            p = head
            while p != slow:                       # phase 2: both move one step
                p, slow = step(p), step(slow)
            return p
    return -1                                      # fast fell off the end: no cycle

bugs: Checking fast.next without first checking fast (null access).
Comparing values instead of node identity.
In phase 2, moving the second pointer two steps instead of one.
For the middle: off by one between the first and second middle on even lengths.

Sort and search.summary: Sort with the right comparator, or partition around a pivot to find the k-th item without a full sort.
signals: "k-th largest / smallest" in average O(n) (quickselect)
Three groups in one pass (Dutch flag: sort colors)
Order items by a custom rule (largest number from digits, h-index)
After sorting, a single scan answers the question
Sort and search.idea: Quickselect partitions the array around a pivot, like quicksort, but then continues only into the side that holds index k. With a random pivot the expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n). For custom orders, write a comparator that decides which of two items goes first (for "largest number", compare a+b with b+a).
Sort and search.example: The k-th smallest value (k from 1) with quickselect.

code.python:
import random

def kth_smallest(a, k):                    # k from 1
    a = list(a)
    lo, hi, target = 0, len(a) - 1, k - 1
    while True:
        p = random.randint(lo, hi)         # random pivot
        a[p], a[hi] = a[hi], a[p]
        store = lo
        for i in range(lo, hi):            # Lomuto partition
            if a[i] < a[hi]:               # CHANGE: the order
                a[i], a[store] = a[store], a[i]
                store += 1
        a[store], a[hi] = a[hi], a[store]  # the pivot is now at its final index
        if store == target:
            return a[store]
        if store < target:
            lo = store + 1                 # keep only the side that holds k
        else:
            hi = store - 1

Sort and search.complexity: O(n) average time, O(n²) worst case, O(1) extra space.
bugs: A fixed pivot (first or last) on sorted input gives O(n²): choose it at random.
Mixing 0-based and 1-based k.
Comparators that are not consistent (a < b and b < a both true).
Recursing into both sides (that is quicksort, O(n log n)).

Math & number theory.summary: A few exact tools: gcd, fast power by squaring, the sieve of primes, and digit-by-digit arithmetic.
signals: Count primes up to n, or test many numbers for primality
Very large exponents, often "modulo 10^9 + 7"
Fractions, ratios, lines through points (reduce with gcd)
Big numbers as strings (multiply strings), base conversion
Math & number theory.idea: The sieve crosses out multiples of each prime p starting at p·p, so all primes up to n cost O(n log log n). Fast power squares the base and halves the exponent: O(log n) multiplications. gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) shrinks quickly. For huge results, take the modulus after every multiplication so numbers stay small.
Math & number theory.example: Sieve of Eratosthenes, fast modular power and gcd.
Math & number theory.complexity: Sieve O(n log log n); power O(log e); gcd O(log min(a, b)).
bugs: Starting the sieve's inner loop at 2p instead of p·p (correct but slower) or at p (wrong).
Overflow in a·b before the modulus: use 64-bit or 128-bit.
Negative exponents in pow(x, n): invert x first, and handle n = -2^31.
Floating-point slopes for collinear points: use reduced (dy, dx) pairs.

String matching.summary: KMP: precompute, for each prefix of the pattern, its longest border, so the search never moves backwards.
signals: Find a pattern in a text in O(n + m)
Longest prefix that is also a suffix ("happy prefix")
Shortest palindrome by adding characters in front (pattern + '#' + reversed)
Repeated substring, string period
String matching.idea: lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. While scanning the text, on a mismatch after j matched characters, jump j back to lps[j-1] instead of restarting: those characters are already known to match. Each text character is looked at a bounded number of times, so the search is O(n + m).
String matching.example: Index of the first occurrence of a pattern in a text (-1 if none).
String matching.complexity: O(n + m) time, O(m) extra space.
bugs: Building lps with i and length moving the wrong way on a mismatch (length = lps[length-1], not length - 1).
Forgetting the empty pattern case (answer 0).
Off by one when reporting the match start (i - m + 1).
Using a rolling hash without checking for collisions.

Tree construction & serialization.summary: The root comes first (preorder) and splits the inorder list into left and right subtrees.
signals: Build a tree from two traversals (preorder + inorder, postorder + inorder)
Serialize a tree to a string and back
Build a balanced BST from a sorted array (the middle is the root)
Flatten a tree into a list in place
Tree construction & serialization.idea: In preorder the first value is the root. Find it in inorder (a hash map from value to index makes this O(1)): everything left of it is the left subtree, everything right is the right subtree, and their sizes tell you where each subtree's preorder part starts. Recurse with index ranges instead of slicing to stay O(n). For serialization, write preorder with a marker for null children; reading it back in the same order rebuilds the tree.
Tree construction & serialization.example: Build a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals (values are distinct).
Tree construction & serialization.complexity: O(n) time with the index map, O(n) space.
bugs: Slicing lists at each level, which makes it O(n²).
Searching inorder linearly for the root each time.
Values that repeat: the index map breaks; the problem must promise distinct values.
Serializing without null markers, which makes the tree ambiguous.

BST operations.summary: Every left value is smaller and every right value bigger, so each step goes down one side.
signals: The tree is a binary search tree
k-th smallest, successor, closest value, range of values
Insert, delete or search a key in O(height)
Lowest common ancestor in a BST (split point of the two keys)
BST operations.idea: Compare the key with the node and go left or right: only one path is visited, so search, insert and delete cost O(height). An inorder walk (left, node, right) visits the keys in sorted order; with an explicit stack you can stop after k nodes for the k-th smallest.
BST operations.example: k-th smallest value in a BST (iterative inorder).

code.python:
def kth_smallest(root, k):             # node: .val, .left, .right
    stack, node = [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:                    # go as far left as possible
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()             # the next value in sorted order
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:                     # CHANGE: what to do with each sorted value
            return node.val
        node = node.right
    return None

BST operations.complexity: O(h + k) time, O(h) stack, where h is the height (log n if balanced, n if not).
bugs: Forgetting that an unbalanced BST has height n.
Deleting a node with two children without replacing it by its successor.
Counting k from 0 instead of 1.
Walking the whole tree when you can stop early.

Minimum spanning tree.summary: Kruskal: take edges from lightest to heaviest, skipping any that would close a cycle.
signals: Connect all points / cities / houses with the least total cost
"Every node must be reachable" and you pay per edge
A virtual node for "build it here" options (wells, power stations)
Which edges are in every / some minimum tree (critical edges)
Minimum spanning tree.idea: Sort the edges by weight. Walk them in order and keep an edge only if union-find says its ends are in different trees; then union them. Stop after n - 1 edges. This is correct because the lightest edge crossing any cut is always safe (the cut property). Prim's algorithm grows one tree with a heap instead and is better for dense graphs.
Minimum spanning tree.example: Minimum total cost to connect n nodes (-1 if impossible).

code.python:
def mst_cost(n, edges):                    # edges: (w, u, v), undirected
    parent = list(range(n))
    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path halving
            x = parent[x]
        return x
    total = used = 0
    for w, u, v in sorted(edges):          # lightest first
        ru, rv = find(u), find(v)
        if ru == rv:
            continue                       # would close a cycle
        parent[ru] = rv
        total += w                         # CHANGE: what to collect
        used += 1
        if used == n - 1:
            break
    return total if used == n - 1 else -1  # -1: not connected
code.scala:
def mstCost(n: Int, edges: Seq[(Int, Int, Int)]): Long = {   // (w, u, v), undirected
  val parent = Array.tabulate(n)(identity)
  def find(x0: Int): Int = { var x = x0; while (parent(x) != x) { parent(x) = parent(parent(x)); x = parent(x) }; x }
  var total = 0L
  var used = 0
  for ((w, u, v) <- edges.sorted if used < n - 1) {           // lightest first
    val (ru, rv) = (find(u), find(v))
    if (ru != rv) { parent(ru) = rv; total += w; used += 1 }   // CHANGE: what to collect
  }
  if (used == n - 1) total else -1
}

Minimum spanning tree.complexity: O(E log E) time for the sort, O(V) for union-find.
bugs: Forgetting to check that n - 1 edges were taken (the graph may be disconnected).
Building all O(n²) edges for points when Prim on the dense matrix is simpler.
Using a plain DFS cycle check per edge (O(E · V)).
Treating the graph as directed.

Knapsack DP.summary: dp[c] = best result with capacity c; loop capacities backward for 0/1 items, forward for unlimited items.
signals: Pick items with a weight / cost limit to maximize value
"Can these numbers make the sum T?" (subset sum, equal partition, target sum)
Count the ways to make an amount (coin change II)
Fewest items to reach a total (perfect squares, coin change)
Knapsack DP.idea: Use a 1-D array over capacities. For each item, update dp[c] = best(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v). With 0/1 items, loop c from high to low so dp[c - w] still means "without this item"; with unlimited items loop from low to high so an item can be reused. For counting ways, put the items in the outer loop (combinations, not orderings).
Knapsack DP.example: 0/1 knapsack: the most value within capacity W, each item used at most once.
bugs: Looping capacities upward for 0/1 items (uses an item twice).
Swapping the loops when counting combinations (you count orderings).
Wrong start value: 0 for max value, -infinity when the capacity must be filled exactly, 1 way for sum 0.
Capacity too large for an array: the DP is pseudo-polynomial.

Grid DP.summary: dp[r][c] for a cell comes from the cells you can arrive from (usually up and left).
signals: Move only right / down (or down a triangle) and count paths or minimize cost
Obstacles that block cells
"Minimum health needed": fill from the end backwards
The grid itself can hold the dp values (in place)
Grid DP.idea: Each cell's best value is its own cost plus the best of the cells you can come from. Fill the first row and column separately (they have only one way in), then the rest row by row. If the answer depends on what comes after (dungeon game), fill from the bottom-right corner backwards. One row of memory is enough because each row only needs the row above.
Grid DP.example: Minimum path sum from the top-left to the bottom-right, moving right or down.
bugs: Forgetting that the first row and column have only one neighbour.
Treating an obstacle as cost 0 instead of unreachable.
Filling forwards when the constraint flows backwards.
Mutating the input grid when the caller needs it.

Dual-sequence DP.summary: dp[i][j] relates the first i of one sequence to the first j of the other: match, skip one, or skip the other.
signals: Two strings: edit distance, interleaving, distinct subsequences, supersequence
"Minimum operations to turn A into B"
"How many ways does B appear in A"
Alignment problems (diff, DNA)
Dual-sequence DP.idea: Look at the last characters a[i-1] and b[j-1]. If they match you can use the diagonal dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise you pay for an operation and move up (drop from A), left (drop from B), or diagonally (replace). Row 0 and column 0 describe one empty string: i deletions or j insertions.
Dual-sequence DP.example: Edit distance (insert, delete or replace one character).
Dual-sequence DP.complexity: O(n · m) time, O(n · m) space (O(m) with two rows).
bugs: Wrong base row: dp[0][j] = j and dp[i][0] = i, not 0.
Adding 1 on a match.
Mixing up which move is insert and which is delete (it does not change the count, but it matters when you list the edits).
Using one rolling row and overwriting the diagonal you still need: keep it in a variable.

Interval DP.summary: dp[i][j] is the answer for the piece s[i..j]; fill by increasing length, trying each split or the two ends.
signals: Palindromes inside a string (longest palindromic subsequence, count palindromic substrings)
Merge or burst things where the order of operations matters (burst balloons, merge stones)
The answer for a range depends on smaller ranges inside it
n up to a few hundred (O(n³) is fine)
Interval DP.idea: dp[i][j] covers only s[i..j]. Ranges of length 1 are the base case. Then for each length from 2 to n and each start i (with j = i + length - 1), combine smaller ranges: either look at the two ends (if s[i] == s[j] use dp[i+1][j-1]) or try every split point k between i and j. Filling by length guarantees the smaller ranges are ready.
Interval DP.complexity: O(n²) time here (O(n³) with a split loop), O(n²) space.
bugs: Filling row by row from the top, so dp[i+1][...] is not ready: loop by length, or i from n-1 down.
Forgetting the base case of length 1 (and length 2 when the ends match).
Off by one in the split loop (k from i to j - 1).
Reading dp[i+1][j-1] when i + 1 > j - 1 (an empty range is 0).

Tree DP.summary: Each subtree returns a small tuple of answers, one per state (taken / not taken, covered / not).
signals: Choose nodes in a tree with a rule between parent and child (no two adjacent, cameras)
"Maximum / minimum over all ways" on a tree
Count structures (unique BSTs) built from smaller ones
A plain DFS return value is not enough: you need the answer under two or three conditions
Tree DP.idea: Post-order DFS returns one value per state of the node. For "no two adjacent": with = node.val + without(left) + without(right); without = best(left) + best(right). The parent combines its children's tuples the same way, and the root's best state is the answer. Each node is solved once: O(n).
Tree DP.example: House robber III: the most money from a tree of houses, never robbing a parent and its child.
bugs: Returning only one number and losing the information the parent needs.
Memoizing on node objects in a map when a tuple return is simpler.
Mixing up which child state goes with which parent state.
Forgetting the null case returns (0, 0).

DP on a DAG.summary: Memoized DFS: the best answer from a state is computed once, from the states it can move to.
signals: Longest path when moves only go "uphill" (increasing values, longer words, divisibility)
The transitions are not a fixed offset like i-1 or i-2
"From each cell / word, how far can you go?"
No cycles are possible, so recursion with a cache terminates
DP on a DAG.idea: Think of each state as a node and each legal move as an edge; because moves only go one way (bigger value, longer word) there are no cycles. Then best(state) = 1 + max(best(next) for each move), computed by DFS with a memo so each state is solved once. Equivalently, process states in topological order (for example sorted by value).
DP on a DAG.example: Longest strictly increasing path in a matrix (moving up, down, left, right).
DP on a DAG.complexity: O(rows · cols) time (each cell and its 4 moves once), O(rows · cols) memo.
bugs: Forgetting the memo, which makes it exponential.
Allowing equal values, which creates cycles and infinite recursion.
Deep recursion on big inputs: raise the limit or iterate in sorted order.
Starting only from one cell instead of taking the best over all starts.

Bitmask DP.summary: The state is a set of used items stored as the bits of an integer: dp[mask].
signals: n is small (up to about 20) and the order or choice of a subset matters
Visit all nodes, assign each worker one task, split into k equal groups
"Smallest team that covers every skill"
2^n · n fits in time (about 2·10^7 for n = 20)
Bitmask DP.idea: Let bit i of mask mean "item i is used". dp[mask] is the best result for exactly that set. To extend a state, try every item i not in mask and move to mask | (1 << i). Process masks in increasing order: adding a bit always makes a bigger number, so the smaller states are ready. Use popcount(mask) when the next step depends on how many items are used.
Bitmask DP.example: Assignment problem: worker k (k = number of tasks already given out) takes one free task; minimize the total cost.

code.python:
def min_assignment(cost):                  # cost[worker][task], n x n
    n = len(cost)
    INF = float("inf")
    dp = [INF] * (1 << n)                  # dp[mask]: tasks in mask are taken
    dp[0] = 0
    for mask in range(1 << n):             # smaller masks first
        if dp[mask] == INF:
            continue
        k = bin(mask).count("1")           # the next worker
        if k == n:
            continue
        for t in range(n):
            if not mask & (1 << t):        # task t is free
                nxt = mask | (1 << t)
                dp[nxt] = min(dp[nxt], dp[mask] + cost[k][t])   # CHANGE: the transition
    return dp[(1 << n) - 1]

bugs: Checking a bit with & 1 << i without parentheses in languages where precedence differs.
Iterating masks in an order where a needed state is not ready.
Using it for n = 30 or more (2^30 states is too many).
Forgetting the infinite start value for unreachable masks.

Segment tree and range queries.summary: A tree over the array where each node stores the answer for a range: update and query in O(log n).
signals: Range sum / min / max queries mixed with updates
"Count of smaller numbers after self", inversions, range counts (index by value)
Many range updates and range queries (lazy propagation)
Prefix sums would need O(n) per update
Segment tree and range queries.idea: Store the array in the leaves of a complete binary tree; each internal node holds the combined value (sum, min, max) of its two children. A point update changes one leaf and recomputes its ancestors. A range query combines the O(log n) nodes that exactly cover the range. This bottom-up version keeps the tree in an array of size 2n: the leaves are tree[n..2n-1] and the parent of i is i // 2.
Segment tree and range queries.example: Range sum query with point updates.

code.python:
class SegTree:                             # sums; leaves are tree[n:]
    def __init__(self, a):
        self.n = len(a)
        self.tree = [0] * self.n + list(a)
        for i in range(self.n - 1, 0, -1):
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[2 * i] + self.tree[2 * i + 1]   # CHANGE: combine

    def update(self, i, value):            # a[i] = value
        i += self.n
        self.tree[i] = value
        while i > 1:
            i //= 2
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[2 * i] + self.tree[2 * i + 1]

    def query(self, l, r):                 # sum of a[l..r), r exclusive
        res = 0                            # CHANGE: the identity value
        l += self.n
        r += self.n
        while l < r:
            if l & 1:
                res += self.tree[l]
                l += 1
            if r & 1:
                r -= 1
                res += self.tree[r]
            l //= 2
            r //= 2
        return res

Segment tree and range queries.complexity: O(n) to build, O(log n) per update and per query, O(n) space.
bugs: Mixing inclusive and exclusive right ends in the query loop.
Forgetting to recompute the ancestors after an update.
The wrong identity value (0 for sum, +infinity for min).
Using a segment tree when the array never changes (prefix sums are simpler).

Divide and conquer.summary: Split the input in halves, solve each half, and do the real work while merging.
signals: Count pairs (i < j) with a condition: inversions, reverse pairs, smaller numbers after self
Merge two sorted results (skyline, k sorted lists)
"Median of two sorted arrays", closest pair, different ways to parenthesize
An O(n²) pair count that should be O(n log n)
Divide and conquer.idea: Recursively sort each half. While merging two sorted halves you can count, in one linear pass, how many pairs cross the middle with the property you want, because both sides are sorted. Every pair is counted at exactly one level of the recursion, so the total is O(n log n).
Divide and conquer.example: Count inversions: pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j].
Divide and conquer.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) extra space.
bugs: Counting the cross pairs after merging instead of before (or in the wrong pass).
Off by one in the split (mid included on both sides).
Overflow: the number of pairs can reach n²/2, use 64-bit.
Copying sub-lists at every level instead of using index ranges and one buffer.

Line sweep and difference arrays.summary: Turn intervals into +1 / -1 events, sort them, and sweep while keeping a running total.
signals: How many intervals overlap at the busiest moment (rooms, cars, bookings)
Many "add v to every index in [l, r]" updates, read once at the end
Events along a time line or x-axis (skyline, rectangle union)
Capacity checks: does the running load ever exceed C?
Line sweep and difference arrays.idea: Each interval [start, end) becomes two events: +1 at start and -1 at end. Sort the events by time (ends before starts at the same time when end is exclusive) and walk them, keeping a running count; its maximum is the answer. For range adds on an array, write +v at l and -v at r + 1 in a difference array and take one prefix sum at the end.
Line sweep and difference arrays.example: Most intervals active at the same time (meeting rooms needed).

code.python:
def max_overlap(intervals):                # intervals [start, end), end exclusive
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))              # CHANGE: weight (passengers, height...)
        events.append((e, -1))
    events.sort()                          # at equal times -1 sorts before +1
    active = best = 0
    for _, d in events:
        active += d
        best = max(best, active)
    return best

def apply_range_adds(n, updates):          # updates: (l, r, v), inclusive
    d = [0] * (n + 1)
    for l, r, v in updates:
        d[l] += v
        d[r + 1] -= v
    out, run = [], 0
    for i in range(n):
        run += d[i]
        out.append(run)
    return out

Line sweep and difference arrays.complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) space. The difference array is O(n + updates).
bugs: Wrong tie order: with [start, end) an end and a start at the same time must not count as an overlap, so process -1 first.
Writing -v at r instead of r + 1 in the difference array.
Forgetting the final prefix pass over the difference array.
Using a sweep when the coordinates are huge and sparse without sorting events (use a map).

Simulation.summary: Do exactly what the statement says, with clean state: position, direction, and a loop.
signals: The statement describes rules step by step (robot moves, text layout, zigzag)
No clever trick is expected; correctness and edge cases are the test
Directions that turn left or right (use a direction array and an index)
Detect a repeat or a cycle in the state to stop early
Simulation.idea: Keep the state small and explicit: for a robot, (x, y) and a direction index into [(0,1), (1,0), (0,-1), (-1,0)]. Turning right is d = (d + 1) % 4, turning left is d = (d + 3) % 4. Run the rules exactly, then look for a shortcut the statement allows (after one pass of the instructions the robot is bounded if it is back home or not facing north).
Simulation.example: Robot bounded in a circle: after repeating the instructions forever, does the robot stay near the start?

code.python:
def is_robot_bounded(instructions):
    dirs = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]  # north, east, south, west
    x = y = d = 0
    for c in instructions:                 # CHANGE: the rules
        if c == "G":
            x, y = x + dirs[d][0], y + dirs[d][1]
        elif c == "R":
            d = (d + 1) % 4
        else:                              # "L"
            d = (d + 3) % 4                # + 3 instead of - 1: never negative
    return (x, y) == (0, 0) or d != 0      # back home, or turned: it loops

Simulation.complexity: O(length of the instructions) time, O(1) space.
bugs: Using (d - 1) % 4 in languages where % can be negative.
Mixing up x/y with row/column.
Simulating forever instead of finding the repeat condition.
Off-by-one in loops over the input.
